newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China raises diesel imports on lower crude runs.
newsitem.headline: China raises diesel imports on lower crude runs.

text.p: China plans to raise its November and December diesel imports by about 100,000 tonnes over October due to a 10-20 percent cut in crude runs, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"Over the past two months our refineries have cut runs by 10-20 percent," a source at state-refiner Sinopec said. Sinopec has a total refining capacity of about 4.1 million barrels per day.

As a result of the reduced refinery operations, China's diesel imports for the last two months of the year is expected to increase to an estimated 600,000 tonnes per month, a source at state-trader Sinochem said.
China diesel imports in October was estimated at 500,000 tonnes.
"We still need to cover some more cargoes for December," the Sinochem trader said.
China earlier this week bought a 30,000-tonne cargo for arrival in mid December at $235 per tonne on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis, traders said.
Sinopec refineries reduced their runs because domestic product prices was not raised to match the higher imported crude oil prices, the source said.

Domestic ex-refinery diesel prices were marginally raised on October 18 by 90 yuan to 1,990 yuan. But some traders said the hike was still insufficient, compared to ther recent rise in crude prices. In late October, the benchmark Brent crude December contract reached a post-Gulf War high at $25.06 a barrel.

China had stopped issuing oil product export licences in 1996 due to the high domestic demand, the source said. Currently product exports from China are solely from processing barrels, the source said.
Sinopec may raise its refinery runs later in the year if imported diesel prices rise substantially, the sources said.
China had paid up to $242 per tonne on a c-and-f basis for its diesel imports in October compared to the latest $235 deal.
If higher international prices rise sharply, "the government will ask Sinopec to increase run capacity to meet domestic market in December or Janaury," the source said.
As result of China's increased purchases and other renewed buying from other regional countries, diesel prices in Singapore have held steady despite falling prices in the west.
Diesel on Tuesday was assessed at $30.80 a barrel free-on-board Singapore, equal to its five-year traded high which was chalked up on earlier this month.
